lesson.title: Access Ports: Where Ordinary Devices Plug In
lesson.summary: An access port is a switch port assigned to exactly one VLAN and configured to send and receive only plain, untagged Ethernet frames, which is exactly what ordinary end devices like laptops and printers expect. It is the everyday counterpart to the trunk port covered in the previous chapter.
lesson.body:
An access port is a switch port assigned to exactly one VLAN, and it deals exclusively in plain, untagged Ethernet frames, the same frame format described all the way back in the very first chapter of this set. It is, in a real sense, the default and most common kind of switch port: any ordinary end device, a laptop, a desktop, a printer, a network camera, plugs into an access port, and that port belongs to one VLAN and one VLAN only. This stands in direct contrast to the trunk port from the previous chapter, which carries tagged traffic for many VLANs across a single link, typically between switches rather than to end devices.

The switch does all the VLAN bookkeeping on the end device's behalf. When an untagged frame arrives on an access port, the switch already knows which VLAN that frame belongs to, simply from the port's static VLAN assignment, so no tag needs to travel over that particular wire at all. Internally, inside the switch's own forwarding logic, the frame is associated with that VLAN from that point forward. If the frame's destination turns out to live across a trunk link on a different switch, the switch is the one that adds the 802.1Q tag, exactly as walked through in the VLAN tagging chapter, right before sending it out across the trunk. And when a switch delivers a frame out to an end device through an access port, it strips off any tag first, handing the device back a plain, ordinary Ethernet frame.

This division of labor is deliberate and mirrors a pattern that shows up elsewhere in switched Ethernet: end devices stay simple, and the switches absorb the complexity. A laptop's network card was built to the plain Ethernet standard and has no idea VLANs exist, no more than it needs to know how a learning switch quietly builds its MAC address table in the background. All of the VLAN machinery, tagging, trunking, and per VLAN forwarding, lives entirely inside the switching infrastructure, invisible to anything plugged into an access port.

Trace one frame through the full path to see the whole picture assembled. A Sales PC plugs into port 3 of switch 1, which is configured as an access port in VLAN 10. The PC sends an ordinary, untagged frame addressed to a Sales printer's MAC address. Switch 1 receives it on port 3 and, because of that port's static VLAN assignment, treats it as VLAN 10 traffic. Consulting its VLAN 10 forwarding table, built earlier through ordinary MAC learning, the switch finds that the printer's address is reachable out its trunk link to switch 2, so it tags the frame with VLAN ID 10 and sends it across. Switch 2 receives the tagged frame on its trunk port, reads the VLAN ID, looks up the destination in its own VLAN 10 table, and finds it maps to port 7, an access port in VLAN 10 where the printer is plugged in. It strips the tag and delivers a plain, untagged frame to the printer, which processes it exactly as though none of this VLAN infrastructure existed at all.

One practical detail worth knowing: on many switches, any port that has not been explicitly assigned to a VLAN still defaults to some standard VLAN, often VLAN 1, rather than being left in an undefined state. This is exactly why deliberately assigning every populated access port to its intended VLAN is considered basic network hygiene: an overlooked, unassigned port can quietly drop a device into the wrong broadcast domain, undoing the careful isolation the rest of this chapter set was built to provide.
